summary: Defines how Diameter agents should route requests when the User-Name contains a Network Access Identifier with multiple realms, called a decorated NAI. These are used to force a request along a chosen path of realms. It clarifies earlier behavior and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A letter's address can list several post offices to go through. This document explains how Diameter helpers should read that list and pass the request along in the right order.

subtitle: How Diameter agents peel a list of realms off a user name so a request visits the realms the user chose.

tldr.problem: A user name can carry several realms to force a request through chosen intermediate networks, but the Diameter base protocol did not say how agents should handle that list.
tldr.mechanism: Each agent that handles the request locally strips its own realm from the decorated NAI in the User-Name AVP, then rewrites User-Name and Destination-Realm to match the next realm before forwarding.
tldr.outcome: Agents can enforce realm-by-realm routing in a backwards-compatible way, with the RFC warning that malformed realm lists can waste routing effort.

today: RFC 5729 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3588. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5729 defines what Diameter agents must do when the User-Name AVP holds a Network Access Identifier (NAI) with several realms, called a Decorated NAI. Decorated NAIs force a request through a predefined list of mediating realms.

The document does not define a new Diameter application. It describes behavior common to any new application that routes requests based on a decorated NAI. RFC 4282 allows multiple realms in an NAI but does not say how Diameter agents should treat them, so this document captures those requirements.
sections.eli5: Some addresses list more than one stop. This document says how the helpers along the way should read such an address.

sections.title: The Routing Problem
sections.content:
RFC 3588 describes request routing only for requests that carry a Destination-Realm AVP. A peer may fill that AVP from the realm in the User-Name NAI. With a decorated NAI, a terminal that knows it must pass through certain realms lists them, followed by the home realm, in its NAI.

The RFC says this replicates NAI-based routing enforcement already used in RADIUS-based roaming networks, and that several 3GPP and WiMAX specifications assume Diameter supports it. The problem has two parts: agents must update both Destination-Realm and User-Name from the decorated NAI, and they must do so in a way that stays compatible with RFC 3588.

Decoration is not limited to network access authentication. It can be used with any Diameter application whose commands are proxiable and include User-Name with an NAI.
sections.eli5: A traveler wants a message to go through certain towns on the way home. The towns need clear rules for handing the message on.

sections.title: Reading a Decorated NAI
sections.content:
Compliant implementations MUST interpret decorated NAIs in a uniform way. The character ! (hexadecimal 0x21) separates the realms in the decorated list, as in the examples in RFC 4282.

For example, a terminal using the route through z.example.com and x.example.com to its home realm h.example.com would use the NAI x.example.com!h.example.com!username@z.example.com. The realm after the @ is the first hop.
sections.eli5: The exclamation marks work like commas in a list of stops. The last name after the at sign is where the message goes first.

sections.title: How Agents Route the Request
sections.content:
A client originating a request sets Destination-Realm to the realm after the @ in the NAI, whether or not the NAI is decorated. When an agent receives a request whose Destination-Realm is a realm it is configured to process locally (and, for proxies, the application is supported), it MUST do some extra steps first.

  • If User-Name is present, the agent MUST check whether it holds a decorated NAI. If not, normal RFC 3588 processing applies.
  • If it is decorated, the agent MUST process the NAI as defined in RFC 4282, update User-Name, and update Destination-Realm to match the new realm.
  • The request is then sent to the next hop using the normal RFC 3588 routing rules.

Answer processing is unchanged and follows Section 6.2 of RFC 3588.
sections.eli5: Each post office crosses its own name off the list, writes the next stop on the front, and passes the letter on.

sections.title: International Characters in Realms
sections.content:
RFC 3588 ties realm names to the Domain Name System, yet an NAI may contain international characters that RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 do not support. The RFC does not try to fix internationalization, but it states assumptions.

  • Conversion to an ASCII-compatible encoding should happen only when the DNS must be queried, not while placing realms in a decorated NAI. The realm in the NAI stays unchanged.
  • Operators are responsible for provisioning the DNS for every realm that may appear in a decorated NAI, so the conversion cannot fail.

The RFC concludes that avoiding international characters in NAI realms is the best way to avoid trouble.
sections.eli5: Names with unusual letters can confuse the address book, so the safest plan is to use plain letters.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content: The decoration-based routing will be supported by any new Diameter application. Agents that do not comply will not advertise support for those new applications and so will be bypassed. In this way the RFC says backwards compatibility with existing implementations, applications and deployments is guaranteed.
sections.eli5: Older helpers who do not know the new rules are simply left off the route, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious node that starts a request, or indirectly causes one, may build a malformed realm list. That could route requests through realms unrelated to the exchange, or through non-existent realms. A request might travel several hops before such a realm is discovered, adding overhead to the routing system.

NAI decoration is used where messages cross one or more AAA brokers or Diameter proxies between the NAS and the server, so end-to-end communication relies on the security properties of those intermediaries.
sections.eli5: Someone could write a silly or fake list of stops, making the letter wander around for nothing. Every post office on the way also has to be trusted.
